title: A versatile laser-machined rf trap for arrays of 100+ ions
authors: Frank G. Schroer, Ilyoung Jung, Thomas W. Burkle, Jack B. Lyons, Joseph W. Van Vlack, Joseph Ezuma, Philip Richerme
abstract: Large ion crystals in diverse geometries are a key resource for quantum simulation experiments. In this work, we introduce a macroscopic rf trap that supports a wide variety of one-dimensional ion configurations as well as lateral two-dimensional crystals with more than 100 ions. Our design is based on precision-machined fused silica wafers that are stacked to form the trap structure. Ten independently biased electrodes provide flexible control over the axial potential, enabling long one-dimensional crystals, isospaced ion strings, split-well chains, and two-dimensional arrays with tunable aspect ratios. We present the design and fabrication process for this trap and demonstrate the ability to tune the radial secular frequencies, detect and compensate micromotion, rotate the principal axes, and characterize trapped ion heating rates. All trap design and documentation files are freely available alongside this work, to facilitate adoption and further development within the ion trap community.
summary: The authors report on the design and experimental realization of a versatile, laser-machined rf Paul trap capable of holding large arrays of ions (100+). By stacking precisely machined fused silica wafers with independently biased electrodes, they achieve unprecedented control over trapping potentials, enabling stable confinement in complex 1D and 2D geometries. This platform significantly advances the hardware required for scaling up quantum simulation experiments using trapped ions.
main_problem: The development of a versatile, macroscopic radiofrequency (rf) trap capable of confining large arrays of ions in various one-dimensional and two-dimensional geometries for quantum simulation.
main_result: The fabricated laser-machined trap successfully supports robust confinement for ion crystals exceeding 100 ions, while demonstrating tunable control over trapping potentials, micromotion compensation, and low heating rates.
method: The authors utilized precision laser machining of stacked fused silica wafers to create ten independently biased electrodes, allowing precise electrical control over the confining potential.
model_or_system: The system is a macroscopic rf Paul trap designed for trapped ions (specifically $^{171}	ext{Yb}^+$). The trapping potential is modeled using finite-element method (FEM) simulations and analyzed via pseudopotential approximations to predict secular frequencies.
key_observables: Radial and axial secular frequencies ($\omega_y, \omega_z$), micromotion modulation index ($ eta$), motional heating rate ($\dot{ ar{n}}$), and the stable geometry of ion arrays (1D chains, 2D crystals).
important_parameters: The trap supports confinement for $N \approx 500$ to $1000$ ions; frequencies can exceed $2\pi 	imes 3.5$ MHz; residual micromotion is shown to be $\lesssim 0.02$.
main_assumptions: The primary limitations are expected to be off-axis micromotion and background gas collisions at room temperature, despite theoretical estimates for very large ion numbers.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the trap's CAD assembly (stacked wafers), predicted equilibrium geometries for various configurations (1D/2D), measured secular frequencies versus RF voltage, and measurements of micromotion modulation.
paper_structure: The paper details the design and fabrication process using laser-machined fused silica. It presents theoretical modeling via FEM and pseudopotential analysis to predict potential shaping. Experimental sections demonstrate trapping capability across various geometries (1D/2D), measure key motional parameters like micromotion and heating rates, and confirm operational stability.
why_interesting: This work represents a significant engineering advance in the physical platform for quantum simulation. The ability to precisely engineer trap potentials using macro-scale machining opens up new regimes of control over ion crystal geometry compared to previous traps.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) Exploded CAD assembly showing the trap substrates, mounting system, and electrical connections. (b) Picture of the mounted substrates and electrical connections; (c) Schematic of the central trapping region, showing the electrode geometry and coordinate axes. Voltages are applied to endcap (END), midcap (MID), and center (CTR) electrodes, which alternate with grounded (GND) electrodes. Simulated electrical potentials in the trapping region predict the ability to confine ions in multiple geometries, including (d) long 1D chains, (e) uniformly-spaced 1D strings, and (f) lateral 2D crystals.

Figure 2. The radial secular frequencies in the y and z directions show an approximately linear dependence on the applied rf voltage. Solid lines are fits of Eq. 3 to the measured data. The inset shows a typical Raman-driven red sideband scan, from which the radial secular frequencies are extracted.

Figure 3. Micromotion modulation index β measured along the z direction, as a function of displacement voltage applied along the (a) x, (b) y, and (c) z trap axes. Zero displacement corresponds to the trap voltages that minimize the observed micromotion. Displacements are applied by asymmetrically biasing electrodes on opposite sides of the trap. Solid lines are fits to the data that include contributions from both intrinsic and extrinsic micromotion.

Figure 4. (a) Simulated trap potentials when the radial principal axes have been rotated to align with the trap coordinate axes. Under these conditions, the wavevector difference ∆⃗k of our Raman beams couples only to the ωz mode. (b) When the principal axes are rotated, the ωz radial mode (blue points) is excited during a Raman red-sideband scan. The ωy mode (red points) is strongly suppressed and requires a 67 times longer Raman pulse duration to achieve similar excitation. (c) When the principal axes are rotated, we measure a center-of-mass heating rate of 257±41 quanta/s for the ωz mode.

Figure 5. Ions trapped in different 1D configurations. (a) A 31-ion chain is trapped by keeping the axial confinement weak relative to the radial confinement. (b) Increasing the center electrode voltage produces a chain with near-uniform spacing. (c) Continuing to increase the center electrode voltage generates a symmetric double-well potential, with weak ion-ion interactions across wells.
